questions.prompt: A team commits a .mcp.json. You want to change one header and test it without touching the shared file, and you do not want your edit reaching anyone else. What do you do?
options: Edit .mcp.json, commit the change, and revert it after testing
Add the same server name at local scope with your version — local beats project, so yours runs and nobody else sees it
Delete .mcp.json, edit, and restore it from git afterwards
Add your version at user scope, then remember to remove it before the next project
questions.explanation: Precedence is local over project, and entries are matched by name, so a same-named local entry shadows the shared one for you alone. That is exactly what the safety valve is for. Options A and C both involve touching or deleting the tracked file, which is the thing you were trying to avoid. Option D nearly works but leaks: user scope loads in every project you open, so the override is live everywhere until you remember to delete it.

questions.prompt: You define a server in project scope with a url and headers, and someone on the team has the same server defined at local scope with only an env var. At runtime, which fields are live?
options: Both — project supplies url and headers, local supplies env
Only the local entry, in full; nothing is taken from the project entry
Local wins for the fields it declares, project fills in the rest
User scope fills the gaps, then project, then local
questions.explanation: Claude Code uses the entire highest-precedence entry and does not merge fields across scopes. Local is highest, so the project entry is ignored completely — including the url it was relying on for the server to work at all. That silent all-or-nothing behaviour is why the debugging advice is 'define the whole server locally, not just the bit you're changing'. Option D has the order backwards and would merge, which is not what happens.

questions.prompt: You commit a .mcp.json for your team. Which change is the one that actually prevents a secret from landing in git history?
options: Put the token in headers with a value like Bearer sk-livesecret-abc123
Put the token in headers as Bearer ${API_KEY} so the committed file holds the variable name and each machine supplies the value
Put the token in headers, then delete it from .mcp.json before the next commit
Put the token in env with the literal value, since env entries are not written to the file
questions.explanation: Expansion works in url, headers, command, args, and env, and ${VAR} / ${VAR:-default} mean the committed file contains no credential — the machine supplies it at load time. Option A is the failure this prevents: once it is in history, rotating the token is a commit plus a PR to a forty-person repo. Option C is not a control, it's a hope. Option D is factually wrong — env values in a committed .mcp.json are written to the file, which is precisely why expansion exists.

questions.prompt: You clone a repo whose .mcp.json defines a stdio server that runs a build script. /mcp shows it pending approval and the tools are absent. You want to use it. What is the correct read of the situation?
options: The server is broken — a cloned repo cannot reach the author's machine to register it
sse servers cannot be approved from a clone, so this config is malformed
Approval is a human gate: a cloned repo cannot approve its own project servers until you accept workspace trust, then approve the server
The server will load on the next restart without any action from you
questions.explanation: Project-scoped servers require approval in an interactive session, and settings committed to the repo — including anything that would auto-enable them — are ignored in an untrusted folder. So pending approval is the system working: a repository cannot hand itself permission to run code on your laptop. Option A confuses config distribution with runtime registration, which is not how any of this works. Option D would mean the gate didn't exist.
